analysis.one_liner: Requires public disclosure of unsafe trucking companies' safety ratings and mandatory enforcement of serious truck safety violations.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the Motor Carrier Safety Act by voice vote on August 3, 1989, but the House never voted on it and it died in committee, with the Transportation Department filing an unfavorable comment on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Transportation Department to publish the safety ratings of trucking companies rated unsatisfactory and to bar those companies from operating commercial trucks until their ratings improved. It would have required safety inspectors to open enforcement actions whenever serious violations were documented, created a nationwide system of random reinspections to verify that cited trucks were actually repaired, and started rulemakings on better truck brakes and making trucks more visible at night. It also doubled criminal penalties, with mandatory minimum prison terms, for distributing drugs within 1,000 feet of a truck stop or highway rest area.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drives on highways shared with commercial trucks: the bill's findings state that relying on voluntary compliance by carriers has not produced acceptable safety [S5]. Motorists gain from public disclosure of which carriers are unsafe, a ban on operating trucks by carriers rated unsatisfactory until they improve, mandatory enforcement of documented serious violations, random reinspections to confirm repairs, and rulemakings on brakes and truck visibility [S5]. Compliant trucking companies also gain by no longer competing against carriers that cut safety corners. Federal safety inspectors gain a guaranteed GS-12 pay grade [S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who shares the road with trucks

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Department to make public, and periodically update, the safety ratings of motor carriers rated unsatisfactory, and to bar such carriers from operating commercial vehicles until they earn at least a conditional rating [S5].

Requires safety personnel to initiate an enforcement action whenever serious violations — including falsified drivers' logs or medical certificates — can be documented, ending reliance on voluntary compliance, which the bill's own findings call inadequate [S5].

Creates a nationwide random reinspection system and certification paperwork to verify that trucks declared out of service were actually repaired, with state penalties for false statements or unreturned forms [S5].
Directs rulemakings on improved braking performance, including antilock systems, and on making trucks more visible to motorists, particularly at night [S5].
Sets civil-penalty criteria for violations posing imminent hazards, requires annual enforcement reports to Congress through 1993, and upgrades field safety inspectors to grade GS-12 [S5].

Aims the drug provisions at the supply of controlled substances to truck drivers: the bill's findings cite studies and hearings that truck stops and rest areas are used to distribute drugs to commercial drivers, whose drug use is called 'an enormous threat' to all motorists [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers with poor safety records pay the most: public shaming through published unsatisfactory ratings, a prohibition on operating trucks until they improve, mandatory enforcement actions, reinspection and certification paperwork, and eventual brake and visibility rules [S5]. Smaller carriers with thin margins bear compliance costs alongside large ones. People convicted of distributing drugs within 1,000 feet of a truck stop or rest area face doubled penalties with at least a one-year mandatory prison term on a first offense, three years to life for repeat offenders, no suspended sentences or probation, and no parole until the minimum is served [S5]. The Department of Transportation would absorb new rulemaking, reporting, and enforcement obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unsafe trucking companies and drug offenders

drawbacks.text: The drug title is a broad mandatory-minimum escalation: 'truck stop' is defined as almost any facility that fuels or services commercial trucks, so ordinary drug offenses anywhere within 1,000 feet of one carry doubled sentences, a one-year minimum, and — for repeat offenders — three years to life with no probation, suspended sentence, or parole until the minimum is served [S5].

The shutdown and rating provisions fall on businesses as well as individuals: a carrier rated unsatisfactory is barred from operating commercial vehicles until reassessed, which can cost jobs at that company, and the Senate softened the reassessment deadline from 12 months to nine partly to ease that burden [S2, S3, S5].

Most of the safety provisions are instructions to write rules rather than rules themselves — brake standards, visibility, reinspection procedures all start as rulemakings or reports — so benefits depend on later regulatory follow-through, and the Department of Transportation filed an unfavorable executive comment on the bill [S5, S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core safety provisions are real but modest — public ratings, a shutdown threat for the worst carriers, mandatory enforcement of documented violations, and reinspections — aimed squarely at an industry whose own record of voluntary compliance Congress found unacceptable [S5]. The harshest and least targeted part is the drug title, which sweeps a wide swath of geography around truck stops into mandatory-minimum sentencing. On balance the bill would have helped the driving public at a cost borne mainly by unsafe carriers, though its practical effect depended on rules the Transportation Department would have had to write — and the Department opposed the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by voice vote, but the House committees never acted, the Transportation Department opposed it, and it died without a House vote, with its last entry pointing to a successor bill, S. 2393.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Exon on April 18, 1989, the bill went to the Senate Commerce Committee, whose Surface Transportation subcommittee held hearings, and the committee reported it favorably with a substitute amendment on July 27, 1989 [S7].
The Senate passed the amended bill by voice vote on August 3, 1989 [S7, S4].

The House received it on September 6, 1989 and referred it jointly to the Public Works and Transportation and Energy and Commerce Committees, which sent it to subcommittees on surface transportation and health and the environment [S7].
On September 14, 1989, the House received an unfavorable executive comment from the Department of Transportation [S7].
No House committee ever reported the bill and the full House never voted on it; the final action in the record, on September 20, 1990, is a cross-reference reading 'See S.2393' [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Motor carriers with poor safety records are better off: no public rating disclosure, no bar on operating trucks, no mandatory enforcement of documented violations, and no reinspection or brake rules from this bill. The Department of Transportation also avoided the bill's rulemaking and enforcement mandates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unsafe motor carriers and the Transportation Department

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor with both Republican and Democratic cosponsors and passed the Senate by voice vote, so no party opposed it on the record; it died in a House controlled by Democrats without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions — published unsatisfactory safety ratings, a ban on operating trucks until a bad rating improves, mandatory enforcement of documented serious violations, random reinspections, and brake and visibility rulemakings — all impose costs on carriers, hitting unsafe operators hardest. The industry's interest in avoiding these costs ran against the driving public's interest in safer trucks, which is why its fate rested on House inaction rather than any floor vote.

industries.industry: Truck stops and roadside rest-area businesses
industries.note: The bill creates a 1,000-foot drug enforcement zone around any facility that fuels or services commercial trucks, doubling criminal penalties there, which concentrates drug enforcement around these businesses. It does not regulate the businesses themselves, so the effect on them is incidental rather than economic.
